analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25 in three steps, but lets benefit-providing employers pay about $1 an hour less.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, sent to a subcommittee in May 2007, and died there without a hearing or vote; Congress instead raised the minimum wage to $7.25 that same year through a separate Democratic bill with no benefit carve-out.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.25 an hour over two years. It included an unusual trade-off: an employer who provided health insurance or child care benefits worth at least $2,500 a year could pay a lower minimum — $5.15 rising to $6.25 instead of $5.85 rising to $7.25. The idea was to reward employers who cover benefits, but it also let those employers substitute benefits for about $1 an hour of cash wages. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Education and Labor Committee, and Congress raised the minimum wage to $7.25 the same year through a separate Democratic bill without the carve-out.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the minimum wage would gain a raise from $5.15 to as much as $7.25 an hour over two years. Workers at firms that provide benefits would gain employer-funded health or child care coverage, though financed by roughly $1 an hour less in cash pay. Employers already offering qualifying benefits would gain the ability to pay $6.25 instead of $7.25 at the top of the schedule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: It raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 in three steps — $5.85, then $6.55 a year later, then $7.25 two years after that — for workers at employers who do not qualify for the alternative rate.
It creates a financial incentive for employers to provide health insurance or child care benefits worth at least $2,500 a year, by letting those employers pay a lower wage rate.
It directs the Secretary of Labor to define which health and child care benefits qualify (including employer contributions to a health insurance plan) and to establish a method for valuing them.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wages would bear the higher wage floor. Workers at firms that take the benefit carve-out would bear it in a subtler way: about $1 an hour of their raise converted into employer-chosen benefits rather than cash.

drawbacks.text: The alternative rate lets an employer providing $2,500 a year in health or child care benefits pay $6.25 instead of $7.25 at the top of the schedule — about $2,000 less in annual cash wages for a full-time worker — so some workers end up below the full minimum, with the difference in benefits of the employer's choosing rather than money they can spend as they wish.

The bill requires the Secretary of Labor to define which health and child care benefits qualify and to set a method for valuing them, creating a complex determination that employers and workers could dispute over what counts toward the $2,500 threshold.

The higher wage floor raises labor costs for employers, an honest cost supporters had to weigh; the benefit carve-out was the bill's answer to that cost, but it comes at the price of a lower effective floor for benefit-providing firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core raise was real and worth having — the federal minimum had been frozen at $5.15 for a decade. But the benefit swap weakens it: a full-time worker whose employer claims the credit takes home about $2,000 less in cash over a year than under the full minimum, with the difference arriving only as employer-chosen benefits and only if the employer opts in. The bill would also have required the Labor Department to define which benefits qualify and how to value them, adding enforcement disputes to a wage floor that works best when it is simple. Congress ultimately delivered the same increase without the carve-out, which suggests the trade was not necessary to get the raise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee and was sent to a subcommittee a few months after introduction, and neither the committee nor the House ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Heather Wilson introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the opening day of the 110th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.

On May 9, 2007 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill drew only three cosponsors, all Republicans, and no House action followed.

The bill would have raised the minimum wage in three steps to $7.25 but would have allowed employers providing at least $2,500 a year in health or child care benefits to pay lower rates, ending at $6.25.

Congress enacted a $7.25 minimum wage in 2007 through the Democratic-led Fair Minimum Wage Act, which President Bush signed in May 2007, without any benefit-based carve-out — so the wage increase this bill sought became law anyway, in a form without the employer discount.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage workers came out ahead: the $7.25 increase was enacted that same year through a separate bill with no benefit carve-out, so employers lost the chance to pay benefit-providing workers $1 an hour below the full minimum.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage workers, via the clean enacted raise

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it moved to a subcommittee in May 2007 and stayed there.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken; all four sponsors were Republicans, and the bill died without action in the Democratic-controlled Education and Labor Committee.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other minimum-wage employers
industries.note: The bill raises the wage floor they must pay, but the alternative rate gives employers who provide $2,500 a year in health or child care benefits a $1-per-hour discount, so firms already offering benefits would pay less than under a clean increase. Their interest in a lower effective floor runs against workers' interest in higher cash wages.

industries.industry: Health insurers and child care providers
industries.note: The bill steers employer money toward health plans and child care benefits by rewarding firms that provide at least $2,500 a year of them, creating new employer-funded demand for both. Workers at those firms would receive the benefits, though financed by a lower cash wage.
